Good morning. It's Thursday, August 27th, 2026. This is The Morning Brief. I'm Jenny.

ANDREW: And I'm Andrew.

JENNY: Nvidia just posted one of the biggest earnings beats of the year and told investors to expect seventy percent revenue growth next year — a number so aggressive that Wall Street analysts on the call sounded stunned.

ANDREW: And in Washington, President Trump says he's paused negotiations with Iran, even as Qatar's prime minister lands in Tehran today for talks of his own. We'll get into what that means for a war now closing in on six months.

JENNY: Let's get into it.

ANDREW: A quick look at the markets. The S and P 500 closed at seven thousand six hundred seventy-seven, up three tenths of a percent and sitting right near its record high. The Dow gained a third of a percent to close above fifty-three thousand five hundred, its third straight day of gains. The Nasdaq led the way, up seven tenths of a percent to just over twenty-six thousand one hundred fifty. That was all before Nvidia's earnings dropped after the bell — more on that in a moment. The ten-year Treasury yield eased to about four point six five percent, down from a twenty-month high near four point seven five just last week. And the thirty-year fixed mortgage rate is tracking around six point seven five percent, according to Mortgage News Daily.

ANDREW: Jenny, that Nvidia number is where we have to start this morning.

JENNY: It is. Nvidia reported after the close yesterday, and the numbers were enormous. Revenue came in at ninety-six point two billion dollars, up a hundred and six percent from a year ago and well ahead of what Wall Street expected. Adjusted earnings were two dollars and twenty-two cents a share, versus the two-oh-nine analysts were looking for.

ANDREW: That's a clean beat. What made it a story that actually moved markets, though?

JENNY: The guidance. Nvidia told investors to expect around seventy percent revenue growth for its next fiscal year — analysts had modeled something closer to forty-four percent. CEO Jensen Huang told investors that actual demand is running even higher than that, but the company's chip supply can only support seventy percent for now. That guidance was so aggressive that veteran analysts on the earnings call sounded almost stunned by it. The stock jumped as much as seven percent in after-hours and premarket trading, and it pulled Nasdaq futures up with it heading into today's session.

ANDREW: So the AI spending story isn't slowing down, at least not yet.

JENNY: Not according to Nvidia's order book. The company's chief financial officer, Colette Kress, said the real constraint right now isn't demand, it's manufacturing capacity at TSMC and a tight supply of the memory chips that go into these AI systems. So even with orders running hot, Nvidia is essentially rationing what it can ship.

ANDREW: That's worth remembering the next time someone says the AI boom is cooling off.

JENNY: Elsewhere in AI, Anthropic's two biggest pending deals are both still exactly that — pending. The company's roughly six to seven billion dollar acquisition of the AI startup Decart still hasn't been signed, though Bloomberg and Calcalist report the two sides are trading advanced drafts and could finalize as soon as next month. And Anthropic's IPO is still sitting behind a confidential filing from June. A public version, targeting a fall listing on the Nasdaq, has been described as imminent for weeks now, but as of this morning it still hasn't shown up.

JENNY: And in the enterprise world, banks are leaning further into AI. Google Cloud launched a version of its Gemini assistant built specifically for financial services this week, and the Dutch bank Rabobank committed up to two billion euros over three years to build out its own AI capabilities. Over in the Netherlands, ABN Amro is also partnering with the French AI lab Mistral to build custom tools. It's part of a broader pattern of banks racing to embed AI into everyday operations before their competitors do, even as regulators in Europe start enforcing new transparency rules that require companies to disclose when customers are talking to a chatbot.

JENNY: Andrew, let's go to you for the national story we've been tracking for months now.

ANDREW: The Iran war is closing in on six months, and there's a real shift to report today. Yesterday, President Trump said the situation is, in his words, "good" — but he also confirmed he's paused U.S. negotiations with Iran, saying talks could resume "at some point." That's a step back from Monday, when Pakistani officials met with Iran's president in Tehran and both sides described real progress toward restoring the ceasefire framework that collapsed back in June.

JENNY: So who's actually talking to Iran right now?

ANDREW: Qatar, as it turns out. The country's prime minister is in Tehran today for meetings with Iranian officials, a diplomatic track that wasn't on the radar even a few days ago. Separately, Iran and Oman appear close to an agreement on a temporary shipping route through the Strait of Hormuz, which has been a flashpoint since an unclaimed strike disabled a tanker near Oman last weekend. At least eighteen U.S. service members have been killed since the war began in late February, and inside Iran, the economic strain is showing too — at least two petrochemical plants in the southwest have suspended production because of heat-driven power shortages.

JENNY: Almost six months in, with the ceasefire framework collapsing once already back in June. Any read on whether this latest push actually holds?

ANDREW: Honestly, that's the question everyone close to this is asking. The June memorandum lasted less than a month before fighting resumed, so officials on both sides are being cautious about calling anything a breakthrough until there's something signed.

ANDREW: In other national news, the Supreme Court this week let a piece of the president's mail-in voting executive order take effect in twenty-three Democratic-led states, ruling six to three along ideological lines. It's a narrower win than it sounds, though. A separate, broader nationwide injunction still blocks the Postal Service from actually implementing the barcoded-envelope and ID rules the order calls for, so nothing changes for voters yet. The administration is now asking the Court to rule on the full merits before the midterms.

ANDREW: And a quick update on the White House ballroom fight. Chief Justice Roberts's administrative stay from last week is still in effect, construction on the roughly four hundred million dollar project is continuing, and the full Court still hasn't ruled on the merits. Two lower courts have already found the project unlawful without congressional approval, so that's the underlying question the justices still have to settle.

ANDREW: Let's shift to home lending, because there's a lot happening with rates this week.

ANDREW: Mortgage rates ticked back up over the last few days, breaking a two-week streak of declines. Daily trackers at Mortgage News Daily have the thirty-year fixed at six point seven five percent as of yesterday, and the Mortgage Bankers Association's own survey has it even higher, at six point seven eight percent, a three-week high. The culprit is a hotter-than-expected inflation reading last week that pushed Treasury yields higher.

JENNY: What about the official weekly number, from Freddie Mac?

ANDREW: That one's actually due out later this morning. Freddie Mac's benchmark survey last had the rate at six point six five percent as of August twentieth, its second straight weekly decline. We'll see if today's reading catches up to what the daily trackers are already showing.

ANDREW: The bigger picture is that buyers are pulling back. The MBA's latest weekly survey showed purchase applications down two percent, and refinancing activity, while up slightly week over week, is still running about eighteen percent below where it was a year ago. HousingWire is also tracking a softer resale market underneath all this — listing inventory has climbed to roughly eight hundred seventy thousand homes nationally, and about forty-two percent of active listings have taken a price cut, a sign sellers are adjusting to buyers who simply can't stretch as far at today's rates.

ANDREW: On the regulatory side, the Federal Housing Finance Agency formally rescinded the bulletin that had directed Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac to police unfair lending practices at the two companies. Director William Pulte says the agency doesn't see itself as a regulator of the GSEs. A separate CFPB rule on mortgage servicing is still expected sometime this month but hasn't landed yet.

JENNY: So the rate picture is basically in limbo until tomorrow?

ANDREW: That's a fair way to put it, and tomorrow is a big reason why. New Fed Chair Kevin Warsh delivers his first Jackson Hole keynote tomorrow morning at the Kansas City Fed's annual gathering in Wyoming, and it could move rates in either direction depending on which way he leans.

ANDREW: Jenny, over to you for Jacksonville.

JENNY: Weather-wise, Jacksonville is looking at low nineties today, with a heat index near a hundred degrees and scattered afternoon thunderstorms. Storm chances only climb from here — sixty percent tomorrow, seventy percent Saturday.

JENNY: At City Hall, the Finance Committee is back at it today for a sixth straight hearing on Mayor Deegan's roughly two billion dollar budget. Wednesday's session ran a full eight hours.

ANDREW: What's driving all the caution on spending?

JENNY: Amendment 3, the homestead exemption question on November's ballot. City auditors estimate it could cost Jacksonville more than three hundred million dollars a year by 2029 if it passes, so Finance Committee chair Will Lahnen has been pushing to preserve cash, and the committee has already trimmed about one percent from the mayor's original proposal and stripped four point nine million dollars in affordable housing funding two weeks ago.

JENNY: There's also an open question at JTA. The transit authority's board met Wednesday to work through naming an interim CEO, internal candidates only, per a decision earlier this month, as outgoing CEO Nat Ford heads to Dallas at the end of October. As of this morning, JTA hasn't publicly announced who got the job, so we'll bring you that as soon as it's official.

JENNY: And down at the stadium, the Jaguars pulled city permits this week for a sales and experience center near the old fairgrounds, part of the broader one point four billion dollar stadium rebuild that's on track to finish in 2028.

ANDREW: Busy few weeks for that project.

JENNY: It really is. One more before we go: City Council voted eighteen to nothing this week on a rule requiring companies that get city economic incentives to make a good-faith effort to hire veterans and military spouses, at least ten percent of new positions, with extra weight given to projects out at Cecil Field. It's a small vote, but it's part of a bigger push to connect Jacksonville's incentive dollars to the region's large military community.

ANDREW: Before we let you go, one thing to watch: tomorrow morning at ten eastern, Fed Chair Kevin Warsh delivers his first Jackson Hole keynote since taking over the central bank. Markets have priced in roughly one-in-three odds of a September rate cut, and Warsh is walking into real tension — solid job growth set against inflation still running near three point seven percent, well above the Fed's target. Watch whether he leans toward the labor market or the inflation number. Either way, expect mortgage rates and the ten-year Treasury to move on it by Friday afternoon.

JENNY: That's your Morning Brief for Thursday, August 27th. Have a great day.

ANDREW: We'll see you tomorrow.

item.title: Jax Morning Brief — Iran Talks "Significant Progress," Nvidia Earnings, JTA Names Interim Chief
item.description: Pakistan reports a breakthrough in Iran war talks even as a tanker is struck near Hormuz. Plus Nvidia's make-or-break earnings, a new JTA interim CEO, and mortgage rates holding in the high sixes.
item.content:encoded:
Good morning. It's Wednesday, August 26th. This is The Morning Brief. I'm Jenny.

ANDREW: And I'm Andrew.

JENNY: Nearly six months into the war with Iran, Pakistan's military says talks in Tehran made significant progress this week toward reviving the ceasefire framework — even as an unclaimed strike disabled an oil tanker near the Strait of Hormuz overnight Monday.

ANDREW: And Nvidia reports earnings after the closing bell today. Wall Street is looking for revenue near ninety-two billion dollars, and it could set the tone for the entire AI trade heading into September.

JENNY: Let's get into it.

ANDREW: A quick look at the markets. The S and P 500 closed at seven thousand six hundred seventy seven, up about a third of a percent. The Dow added roughly one hundred sixty points, also up three tenths of a percent, its third straight winning session. The Nasdaq gained about six tenths of a percent on strength in tech and healthcare. The ten-year Treasury yield sits at about four point seven percent. The thirty-year fixed mortgage rate is tracking in the high sixes — Freddie Mac's weekly survey had it at six point six five percent last Thursday, its second straight weekly decline, while daily trackers like Mortgage News Daily are running a bit hotter, closer to six point seven eight percent. And notably, oil prices actually fell yesterday, even after that tanker was hit off Oman. Traders seem to be pricing in the diplomatic progress out of Tehran more than the attack itself.

ANDREW: Let's start with that diplomacy, because it's the most significant movement we've seen in this war in weeks.

ANDREW: Pakistan's army chief, Field Marshal Asim Munir, and Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi spent Monday in Tehran meeting with President Pezeshkian, and both sides are calling it significant progress toward restoring the Islamabad memorandum — the framework the US and Iran signed back in June to calm the war and reopen shipping through Hormuz, before it collapsed over disputes about who controls the strait.

JENNY: So what actually changed? Because "significant progress" is something we've heard before, and then it falls apart again.

ANDREW: Fair skepticism. The concrete piece is that Iran's core demand — a US recommitment to the section of that agreement governing Iranian arrangements for the strait — is now being carried back to Washington through Pakistan as the formal channel. That's a specific, actionable ask, not just a friendly meeting. For context, the last time we heard language this optimistic was back in June, when the two sides first signed that memorandum, and it held for barely a month before collapsing into two more weeks of fighting in July. So the skepticism is earned. But the risk on the ground hasn't gone anywhere. Overnight Monday, an unidentified projectile disabled a tanker a few miles off Oman's coast. The crew is safe, but nobody has claimed responsibility, and the Pentagon still counts at least eighteen US service members killed since this war began in February.

ANDREW: Separately, the White House is moving toward a new tariff on China, reportedly around seven and a half percent, aimed at what officials call overcapacity — Beijing flooding global markets with underpriced goods. It would push the overall US tariff rate on Chinese imports back toward twenty percent, and it's landing just weeks before a planned summit between President Trump and Xi Jinping.

JENNY: Right before a summit with Xi — that's a pretty pointed message to send.

ANDREW: It is, though officials describe it as calibrated to stay within the boundaries Beijing has already accepted as part of the existing trade truce, not to blow it up. We'll know more as the summit gets closer.

ANDREW: One more thread worth flagging on the economic data front. Growth actually accelerated last quarter, with the economy adding roughly 334,000 net new jobs. But the Fed's preferred inflation gauge also ticked up, running close to 3.7 percent over the past year, well above the central bank's 2 percent target. That combination, stronger growth alongside stickier inflation, is exactly the tension Kevin Warsh has to address on Friday.

JENNY: Which makes his speech even harder to read ahead of time.

ANDREW: That's the view from Washington and Tehran. Jenny, what's happening back home in Jacksonville?

JENNY: Weather-wise, Jacksonville is looking at a hot, stormy one today — a high near ninety-three, with an 80 percent chance of afternoon thunderstorms and lows in the mid-seventies tonight.

JENNY: Closer to home, the Jacksonville Transportation Authority's board meets today and is expected to name an interim CEO — the first concrete step in replacing Nat Ford, who's leaving for Dallas Area Rapid Transit this fall.

ANDREW: Remind me — why is Ford leaving, and who's actually in the running?

JENNY: He was named to lead Dallas's transit agency back on July 21st and starts there October 26th. As for who's next, the JTA board has been clear from the start that it wants to keep this internal — no outside names being considered for the interim role — so today's pick will be a sitting agency executive stepping up while a national search firm looks for a permanent successor. And the backdrop matters here: JTA is also sitting on a projected thirty-one point eight million dollar deficit for this fiscal year, so whoever steps in inherits a real budget problem on day one.

JENNY: Also today, the city council's finance committee is back at it, a full day of budget hearings at City Hall as members work through Mayor Deegan's roughly two billion dollar spending plan. Chair Will Lahnen has been pushing a preserve-cash message all month, largely because of what's on the ballot in November — a proposed increase to the homestead exemption that city auditors estimate could cost Jacksonville more than three hundred million dollars a year in lost revenue by 2029. This is one of several hearings the committee has scheduled this week alone, as members try to lock in savings now in case that ballot measure passes in November.

ANDREW: That's a lot of budget planning happening under a pretty big question mark.

JENNY: It really is. And Jaguars fans headed to EverBank Stadium this season should brace for a construction zone. The team's one point four billion dollar Stadium of the Future project is underway, and capacity is down to about forty-two thousand seats this year, roughly 62 percent of normal, while crews install the steel trusses for a new canopy roof. The stadium is expected to grow to around seventy thousand seats once the project wraps in 2028.

JENNY: And in a smaller but very Jacksonville story this morning, News4Jax is reporting that an abandoned sailboat has been anchored for weeks in the exact spot a sixty-year-old marine towing company needs to move its equipment on the river, effectively freezing part of that family business's operations until the boat gets cleared out.

ANDREW: Sixty years in business, stopped cold by one abandoned boat.

JENNY: Andrew, speaking of big numbers, what's happening on the mortgage side this week?

ANDREW: Rates are holding fairly steady in that high-six range we mentioned earlier, and the Mortgage Bankers Association's latest weekly survey shows demand basically flat — applications down about half a percent for the week, with purchase activity down two percent and refinancing still running around 18 percent below year-ago levels, even though it ticked up slightly week to week.

JENNY: So what does that actually mean for someone trying to buy a house right now?

ANDREW: Nationally, it means demand stays soft as long as rates sit above six and a half percent. But here in Jacksonville specifically, it's actually a fairly balanced market — local listing data has the median sale price around three hundred ten thousand dollars, with roughly four months of inventory on hand. That's enough supply that buyers have real room to negotiate, which isn't true everywhere in the country right now. New listings are also moving at a reasonable clip, spending about a month on market on average, so it's a healthier local picture than the national headlines about soft demand might suggest.

ANDREW: On the regulatory side, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's own agenda points to a final rule on mortgage servicing landing as soon as this month, part of a broader push under an executive order aimed at cutting compliance costs for lenders. And the Federal Housing Finance Agency has pulled back an earlier directive telling Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac to police unfair lending practices themselves, with FHFA's director arguing that enforcement belongs with the Federal Trade Commission, not the mortgage giants. Regulators also quietly raised the dollar threshold that triggers extra appraisal requirements on higher-priced loans, from thirty-three thousand five hundred dollars to thirty-four thousand two hundred, a small but real easing on paperwork costs for some borrowers and lenders.

ANDREW: Jenny, over to you for what's happening in AI and tech.

JENNY: Anthropic's roughly six to seven billion dollar deal to acquire the Israeli AI infrastructure startup Decart still hasn't been signed. The two sides are reportedly trading advanced drafts, with a signing possible as soon as next month.

ANDREW: What does Decart actually do that's worth that kind of money?

JENNY: They build software that helps AI chips run more efficiently, cutting the cost of training and operating large models. For a company burning through enormous amounts of compute, that's a strategic buy aimed at controlling costs, not just picking up talent. It's also notable timing, because Anthropic is separately gearing up for an IPO — it confidentially filed paperwork with the SEC back in June, and reports suggest the public filing could come within days, targeting a Nasdaq listing this fall. That confidential filing came just weeks after Anthropic closed a sixty-five billion dollar funding round that valued the company at nearly a trillion dollars, so whenever this IPO actually lands, it's shaping up to be one of the largest in history.

JENNY: And tonight is the big one for the whole AI trade. Nvidia reports its fiscal second-quarter results after the closing bell. Wall Street is looking for revenue of about ninety-two billion dollars, which would be up roughly 97 percent from a year ago. However this print lands, it tends to set the tone for tech stocks for days afterward.

ANDREW: We'll have the numbers for you tomorrow morning either way.

JENNY: Fair, though if history is any guide, the stock's reaction over the following days tends to matter more than the headline number itself.

JENNY: One more data point on how AI is actually landing inside big companies. Protiviti's latest global finance survey found the share of finance teams using AI for forecasting jumped from 58 percent to 76 percent over the past year. But only about a third of those organizations say they can actually measure whether that investment is paying off, and security and data privacy remain finance leaders' top concern heading into next year, even as AI budgets keep climbing. Adoption is outrunning proof that it works.

ANDREW: Before we let you go, one thing to watch this week. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh delivers his first Jackson Hole keynote Friday morning at 10 AM Eastern, with markets currently pricing in roughly one-in-three odds of a rate move at next month's Fed meeting. Watch whether he leans toward inflation-fighting language or signals any openness to cutting. His tone in that speech could move Treasury yields, and mortgage rates, more than anything else happening this week.

JENNY: That's your Morning Brief for Wednesday. Have a great day.

ANDREW: We'll see you right back here tomorrow morning.
